newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to seek $1 billion to pay off debts to UN.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to seek $1 billion to pay off debts to UN.

text.p: President Bill Clinton will ask Congress for $1 billion to pay off most of the money the United States owes the United Nations, sources at the world body said, confirming a report in Tuesday's Washington Post.
The money was part of a proposed, substantial overall increase in spending on international affairs, the Post said, quoting administration and congressional sources.
Most of the extra money for the United Nations would be appropriated now, but payment would be held back as a way of pressing for U.S.-backed reforms, the newspaper said.
In addition, Clinton would seek to increase foreign affairs spending and foreign aid by about $1.2 billion above this year's level of $18.1 billion, the Post said.

Washington owes the United Nations more than $1 billion and diplomats last week said Clinton would propose paying nearly the entire amount, although it was doubtful this would be approved by the Republican-dominated Congress.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher last week said payment of America's debt to the United Nations was "at the top" of the Clinton administration's agenda in 1997.

Officials told the Post that Clinton felt international affairs spending has been cut too far already and further reductions would undermine the ability of the United States to carry out effective diplomacy.
Under the plan to repay the United States' huge outstanding debt, Washington would repay $100 million in the coming year.
The remaining $900 million would be appropriated now, but held back until 1999 as a lever to ensure that new U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan carries out substantial reforms.
For the United States reform means deep cuts in personnel while for Annan the emphasis is on restructuring the world body to make it more efficient and viable.
Annan, according to Eckhard, would continue to reduce the size of the world body "but nothing like what some members of Congress have proposed."

"The secretary-general has said that reform does not really mean reduction. Reform means building a consensus of what the organization is supposed to do once there is agreement and getting everyone to pay to achieve those objectives," he said.
